title: What a Fluorescent Tag Can Tell You
endLine: Fluorescent tags reveal where proteins go and when signals change.

scenes.tts: Where does a protein go inside a living cell? Look at this branch of a nerve cell. Those green dots mark places we can see because a protein carries its own fluorescent tag.
scenes.caption: Where does a protein go inside a living cell? Look at this branch of a nerve cell. Those green dots mark places we can see because a protein carries its own fluorescent tag.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Throughout, use high-contrast labels in the safe frame and let the subject fill most of the frame height. Leave room for separate captions and keep the cell field subtly drifting between actions. Open on a nerve cell branch with drifting green flecks giving way to settled green dots. Put the spoken question on screen from the first frame as the short label ‘Where does it go?’ Keep the branch large and center it for the push into the next scene. Across the film, use short moving visual holds around the narration to bring the cut up to the web runtime in the brief.
scenes.narration: Where does a protein go inside a living cell? Look at this branch of a nerve cell. Those green dots mark places we can see because a protein carries its own fluorescent tag.

scenes.tts: Green fluorescent protein, or G F P, gives off green light when blue light shines on it. Join its gene to another protein's gene. The cell makes the other protein with G F P attached, so green light marks its location.
scenes.caption: Green fluorescent protein, or GFP, gives off green light when blue light shines on it. Join its gene to another protein's gene. The cell makes the other protein with GFP attached, so green light marks its location.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Zoom into the same branch. Below it, bring two plain gene strips together, then transform them into a plain scaffold shape carrying a green tag. Sweep a blue beam over the tagged protein and let the tag glow green as it settles.
scenes.narration: Green fluorescent protein, or GFP, gives off green light when blue light shines on it. Join its gene to another protein's gene. The cell makes the other protein with GFP attached, so green light marks its location.

scenes.tts: Here the tagged protein is gephyrin. It forms a scaffold beneath inhibitory synapses, the places where one cell can quiet another. Pull back and the tags reveal rows of bright dots along the nerve cell's branching extensions.
scenes.caption: Here the tagged protein is gephyrin. It forms a scaffold beneath inhibitory synapses, the places where one cell can quiet another. Pull back and the tags reveal rows of bright dots along the nerve cell's branching extensions.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Slide the attached green tag and gephyrin shape beneath a synapse contact. Pull back along the same branch as matching green dots come into view along its length. Use ‘Gephyrin’ to identify the scaffold and keep the visible dots tied to their contacts.
scenes.narration: Here the tagged protein is gephyrin. It forms a scaffold beneath inhibitory synapses, the places where one cell can quiet another. Pull back and the tags reveal rows of bright dots along the nerve cell's branching extensions.

scenes.tts: A fluorescent protein can show where something is or report a signal that changes. Calcium acts as a messenger inside cells. One calcium sensor links cyan and yellow fluorescent proteins at opposite ends. Between them sit a calcium-binding protein called calmodulin and a short piece it can grip.
scenes.caption: A fluorescent protein can show where something is or report a signal that changes. Calcium acts as a messenger inside cells. One calcium sensor links cyan and yellow fluorescent proteins at opposite ends. Between them sit a calcium-binding protein called calmodulin and a short piece it can grip.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Follow the camera inward from a bright dot and let the green tags recede. Bring the calcium sensor into the same intracellular field as two separated colored blocks, cyan and yellow, linked to plain central shapes. Highlight each central shape as it is introduced. Keep color roles fixed throughout.
scenes.narration: A fluorescent protein can show where something is or report a signal that changes. Calcium acts as a messenger inside cells. One calcium sensor links cyan and yellow fluorescent proteins at opposite ends. Between them sit a calcium-binding protein called calmodulin and a short piece it can grip.

scenes.tts: When calcium rises, it binds calmodulin, which grips that short piece and pulls the ends close. Shine light that excites cyan. With yellow close by, some energy passes from cyan to yellow, making yellow brighter and cyan dimmer.
scenes.caption: When calcium rises, it binds calmodulin, which grips that short piece and pulls the ends close. Shine light that excites cyan. With yellow close by, some energy passes from cyan to yellow, making yellow brighter and cyan dimmer.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Bring calcium dots into the field. Let one plain middle shape grip its partner and pull the two colored ends close. Bathe the whole sensor in excitation light that excites the cyan end, then move an energy pulse from cyan to yellow so yellow brightens while cyan dims. Keep the sensor large and show the grip before naming it.
scenes.narration: When calcium rises, it binds calmodulin, which grips that short piece and pulls the ends close. Shine light that excites cyan. With yellow close by, some energy passes from cyan to yellow, making yellow brighter and cyan dimmer.

scenes.tts: To track the change, divide the yellow brightness by the cyan brightness. This ratio rises when calcium rises. If calcium drops and the ends move apart, what should happen to the ratio?
scenes.caption: To track the change, divide the yellow brightness by the cyan brightness. This ratio rises when calcium rises. If calcium drops and the ends move apart, what should happen to the ratio?
scenes.visual: Schematic. Extend a readout from the same sensor with ‘Yellow brightness’ over ‘Cyan brightness’ as the narrator describes division. Indicate the rise without numerical values. Leave the sensor close and the prediction visible as ‘What happens to the ratio?’
scenes.narration: To track the change, divide the yellow brightness by the cyan brightness. This ratio rises when calcium rises. If calcium drops and the ends move apart, what should happen to the ratio?

scenes.visual: Schematic. Hold the same sensor and ‘What happens to the ratio?’ for the thinking pause. Let the background drift gently with the state and readout held until narration returns.

scenes.tts: As calcium drops, the grip loosens and the ends separate. Less energy passes from cyan to yellow. Yellow gives off less light relative to cyan, so yellow brightness divided by cyan brightness falls. The readout follows how much the sensor's ends come together.
scenes.caption: As calcium drops, the grip loosens and the ends separate. Less energy passes from cyan to yellow. Yellow gives off less light relative to cyan, so yellow brightness divided by cyan brightness falls. The readout follows how much the sensor's ends come together.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Let calcium dots drift away, release the grip and separate the same ends. Fade the moving energy pulse and dim yellow relative to cyan. Move the indicator down beside the fraction without adding values.
scenes.narration: As calcium drops, the grip loosens and the ends separate. Less energy passes from cyan to yellow. Yellow gives off less light relative to cyan, so yellow brightness divided by cyan brightness falls. The readout follows how much the sensor's ends come together.

scenes.tts: For a location measurement, the tag itself can get in the way. Some proteins carry an address at their very end. That address sends them to compartments called peroxisomes. A tag placed after it can hide it.
scenes.caption: For a location measurement, the tag itself can get in the way. Some proteins carry an address at their very end. That address sends them to compartments called peroxisomes. A tag placed after it can hide it.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Fold away the ratio readout and bring back the green tag beside a plain protein shape. Show its tip address guiding the protein toward a peroxisome, then reset the path before sliding the tag over the address at the tip.
scenes.narration: For a location measurement, the tag itself can get in the way. Some proteins carry an address at their very end. That address sends them to compartments called peroxisomes. A tag placed after it can hide it.

scenes.tts: To guard against that, put the tag where the address stays exposed. Then use a marker that shows where the peroxisomes are. Check whether the tagged protein and the marker light up the same spots.
scenes.caption: To guard against that, put the tag where the address stays exposed. Then use a marker that shows where the peroxisomes are. Check whether the tagged protein and the marker light up the same spots.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Slide the green tag inward so the address is clear at the tip. Pull back to the compartment and overlay distinct peroxisome marker outlines on the same field to demonstrate how to check for overlap. Present the overlay as a check, with no experimental result.
scenes.narration: To guard against that, put the tag where the address stays exposed. Then use a marker that shows where the peroxisomes are. Check whether the tagged protein and the marker light up the same spots.

scenes.tts: Miyawaki, Tsien and colleagues published that color-shifting calcium sensor, called cameleon, in nineteen ninety-seven. Its shifting balance of yellow and cyan gave researchers a way to follow calcium inside a cell. Fluorescent tags can also measure protein amounts in single cells.
scenes.caption: Miyawaki, Tsien and colleagues published that color-shifting calcium sensor, called cameleon, in 1997. Its shifting balance of yellow and cyan gave researchers a way to follow calcium inside a cell. Fluorescent tags can also measure protein amounts in single cells.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Zoom back to the interior and return to the same cyan and yellow sensor. Let the signal change once as the readout follows. Replace the sensor view with a living cell outline as the narration turns to measuring protein amounts.
scenes.narration: Miyawaki, Tsien and colleagues published that color-shifting calcium sensor, called cameleon, in 1997. Its shifting balance of yellow and cyan gave researchers a way to follow calcium inside a cell. Fluorescent tags can also measure protein amounts in single cells.

scenes.tts: In twenty fifteen, Kurt Schmoller, Jan Skotheim and colleagues tagged a protein called Why five. They measured it in single living cells. At birth, small daughter cells had about as many Why five molecules as larger cells. In less space, that made Why five more concentrated.
scenes.caption: In 2015, Kurt Schmoller, Jan Skotheim and colleagues tagged a protein called Whi5. They measured it in single living cells. At birth, small daughter cells had about as many Whi5 molecules as larger cells. In less space, that made Whi5 more concentrated.
scenes.visual: Schematic. Carry the living cell outline forward and use it to compare a small daughter cell and a larger cell. Fill both with about the same number of drifting green dots for tagged Whi5. Bring attention to their closer spacing in the smaller cell. Use no counts or scale.
scenes.narration: In 2015, Kurt Schmoller, Jan Skotheim and colleagues tagged a protein called Whi5. They measured it in single living cells. At birth, small daughter cells had about as many Whi5 molecules as larger cells. In less space, that made Whi5 more concentrated.
